compositions.title: The fisherman and his companion
compositions.text: Se fiscere and his gefēra standað on ðǣm strande. Se gefēra cwið: “Saga mē, hwæt ðū hæbbe.” Se fiscere sægð, ðæt hē męte hæbbe. Hē hǣtt his gefēran ðone fisc beran. Se gefēra birð ðone fisc. Se fiscere cwið: “Ic gesēo ðē ðone fisc beran. Nū wāt ic, ðæt ðū mē hilpst.”
compositions.scope_note: A newly composed connected exchange: request for information, report, instruction, carrying action and observation. Fiscere becomes productive through the assigned Cook vocabulary; all other lexical material is already productive. The hē/his sequence continues the fisherman as the speaker/commander, while the companion carries the fish. Subjunctive hæbbe in an embedded question/report contrasts with asserted indicative hilpst after knowing. The passage does not use the still citation-only infinitive witan or the still supplied adjective geong.

teaching_examples.text: Saga mē, hwæðer ðā męnn gearwe sīen.
teaching_examples.target: A request for the answer to a yes/no question; hwæðer is invariant whether, not the agreeing which-of-two adjective.

teaching_examples.text: Se mann hēt hine ðone fisc beran.
teaching_examples.target: Accusative hine is the commanded actor; the fish is the infinitive's separate accusative object.

teaching_examples.text: Ic gesēo ðone mann ðone fisc beran.
teaching_examples.target: The observer sees the man performing the action; two accusatives have distinct functions.
Gōdne predicates a quality of the accusative object, not of the nominative subject; based on the independently audited gewyrcean frame.
The speaker is not king; a present unreal wish, not an ordinary statement about a past reign.
The finite subject is also the understood actor of the plain infinitive; compare the newly taught separate-actor command frame.
